courseTitle: Python & Scientific Computing for Quantum Applications

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's Hadamard-on-|0> example in a Python script, then modify it to apply the Pauli-X gate to |0> instead and print the resulting state and probabilities, confirming they match the expected deterministic [0,1] outcome rather than Hadamard's 50/50 split.
slots.deliverable: The printed state vector and probabilities for X applied to |0>, with a one-sentence comparison to the Hadamard example's 50/50 result.

lessons.title: Setting Up a Scientific Python Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Create a venv named .venv, activate it, install numpy, scipy, matplotlib, and jupyter via pip, write a requirements.txt pinning the exact installed versions (using pip freeze), and run the lesson's import-and-print-versions script to confirm the environment works.
slots.deliverable: The terminal output of the import/version-check script, plus the generated requirements.txt file listing pinned versions.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the Qubit class from the lesson, instantiate Qubit(0.6, 0.8), call probabilities() and print its repr, then chain a Pauli-X apply_gate call onto the result and print the new Qubit's repr, confirming apply_gate returns a fresh object rather than mutating the original.
slots.deliverable: The printed probabilities, the __repr__ output before and after applying X, and confirmation that the original Qubit object was left unchanged after apply_gate.

slots.practicalActivity: In a real Jupyter notebook, define a variable in one cell and use it in a later cell, deliberately run the cells out of page order to produce a working-but-fragile notebook, then use Kernel > Restart & Run All to see whether it still works, fixing the cell order if it fails.
slots.deliverable: A short written account of what broke (or didn't) under Restart & Run All, and the final cell order that makes the notebook work top-to-bottom.

slots.practicalActivity: Create probs = [0.25, 0.25, 0.5] as a plain Python list and run probs * 100, observing the list-repetition behavior. Then convert it to np.array(probs) and run the same multiplication, confirming it now produces the intended percentage values.
slots.deliverable: Both outputs (the broken list repetition and the correct NumPy element-wise result), with a one-line explanation of why converting to np.array fixed it.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the Pauli matrices X, Y, Z and the Hadamard gate as NumPy arrays, compute X @ Z and Z @ X to confirm they are exact negatives of each other, then compute Y.conj().T and confirm it reconstructs Y itself, showing Y is Hermitian.
slots.deliverable: The computed X@Z and Z@X matrices showing the sign flip, plus the Y.conj().T result confirming it equals Y.

slots.practicalActivity: Using np.linalg.eigvalsh, compute the eigenvalues of M=[[2,1],[1,2]], then verify by hand with the trace/determinant formula that they equal 3 and 1, and confirm the eigenvalue-3 eigenvector directly via M @ v == 3*v.
slots.deliverable: The NumPy-computed eigenvalues, the by-hand trace/determinant derivation showing they match, and the M@v=3v verification for the eigenvalue-3 eigenvector.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the CNOT gate from the lesson's projector formula (np.kron(P0,I) + np.kron(P1,X)), confirm it matches the standard CNOT matrix, then apply it to the state |01> (encoded via np.kron) and confirm the output is unchanged since the control qubit is |0>.
slots.deliverable: The constructed CNOT matrix, and the result of CNOT @ |01> confirming it remains |01>.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lab's own check-yourself exercise: test whether G=[[1,1],[0,1]] is unitary by computing G @ G.conj().T in NumPy and comparing it to the identity with np.allclose, stating explicitly what result would prove G is NOT a valid quantum gate.
slots.deliverable: The computed G @ G.conj().T matrix, the np.allclose(..., np.eye(2)) result, and a written conclusion on whether G is a valid gate.

lessons.title: Complex Numbers in Python
lessons.chapterTitle: Complex Number & Matrix Computation in Python

slots.practicalActivity: For the state (|0> - j|1>)/sqrt(2), compute amp0 and amp1 in Python using the built-in complex type, then compute abs(amp1)**2 and confirm it equals 0.5 (same as the plus-version), explaining in writing why the minus sign didn't change the probability.
slots.deliverable: The computed amp0, amp1, and abs(amp1)**2 values, plus a written explanation of why negating j doesn't change the squared-magnitude probability.

lessons.title: Unitary & Hermitian Checks in Code
lessons.chapterTitle: Complex Number & Matrix Computation in Python

slots.practicalActivity: Write the is_unitary and is_hermitian functions from the lesson, then run both Pauli-X and Pauli-Z through is_hermitian, confirming both return True, and explain in writing why conjugate transpose reduces to plain transpose for matrices with no imaginary entries.
slots.deliverable: The is_unitary/is_hermitian function code, the True/True results for X and Z, and a written explanation of why real matrices' Hermitian check reduces to a symmetry check.

lessons.title: Numerical Precision & Floating-Point Pitfalls
lessons.chapterTitle: Complex Number & Matrix Computation in Python

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's broken_total=0.85 example, run np.isclose(broken_total, 1.0, atol=0.2) to confirm it incorrectly passes, then re-run it with the NumPy default tolerance to confirm it correctly fails, and write a short explanation of what real bug the loosened tolerance would hide.
slots.deliverable: Both isclose results (loose tolerance passing, default tolerance failing) and a written explanation of the danger of loosening tolerances to make a check pass.

lessons.title: Complex Matrix Computation Lab
lessons.chapterTitle: Complex Number & Matrix Computation in Python

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lab's check-yourself matrix B=[[0,2-2j],[2+2j,0]], compute its trace and determinant by hand, solve the resulting quadratic for its eigenvalues, and confirm with np.linalg.eigvalsh that both come out real.
slots.deliverable: The by-hand trace/determinant/quadratic derivation of B's eigenvalues and the matching np.linalg.eigvalsh output confirming they are real.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the two-waveform plot from the lesson (cos(x) and sin(x) with labels, title, and legend) using plt.subplots, then deliberately remove the label= argument from one .plot() call and observe it disappear from the legend, confirming the lesson's check-yourself diagnosis.
slots.deliverable: A saved plot image of the two-curve plot with both legend entries showing, plus a note confirming what happened when one label= was removed.

slots.practicalActivity: Given four squared amplitudes [0.15, 0.35, 0.1, 0.42], sum them first to check normalization before plotting anything and state whether they pass, then build the 4-bar |00>/|01>/|10>/|11> probability chart with annotated values exactly as the lesson demonstrates.
slots.deliverable: The normalization-sum check with a pass/fail conclusion, and the saved 4-bar annotated probability chart.

lessons.title: Visualizing a Qubit State on the Bloch Sphere

slots.practicalActivity: Compute the Bloch coordinates (x,y,z) for the |+i> state (alpha=1/sqrt(2), beta=i/sqrt(2)) using the amplitude-based formulas, confirm the result lands at (0,1,0) as the lesson's table predicts, then draw the wireframe sphere and quiver arrow for this state.
slots.deliverable: The computed (x,y,z) for |+i> confirming (0,1,0), and a saved plot showing the Bloch sphere with the |+i> arrow drawn on the y-axis.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lab's check-yourself scenario — a 2-qubit state with P(00)=0.4, P(01)=0.1, P(10)=0.1, P(11)=0.4 and N=2000 shots — compute all four expected counts by hand, then call the lesson's plot_expected_counts function with the correct labels/probabilities/n_shots arguments to produce the chart.
slots.deliverable: The four hand-computed expected counts and the resulting 4-bar expected-count chart.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's default_rng(42) example twice to confirm identical sequences, then re-run it with seed 7 to confirm a different sequence, and write a one-paragraph answer to the lesson's labmate scenario explaining exactly which code change fixes non-reproducible measurement histograms.
slots.deliverable: Both generator outputs (matching for seed 42 twice, different for seed 7) and a written fix recommendation for the labmate's reproducibility complaint.

slots.practicalActivity: Create the project folder layout from the lesson (src/, tests/, notebooks/, results/, requirements.txt, .gitignore) on disk, move a HADAMARD constant and apply_gate function into src/gates.py, and write and run the test_hadamard_on_zero_gives_equal_superposition test from the lesson, confirming it passes.
slots.deliverable: A listing of the created folder structure, the src/gates.py file contents, and the passing test output.

slots.practicalActivity: Compute the fidelity between psi=[0.6,0.8] and phi=[1,0] as the lesson does, then write two versions of the result: a bare 'fidelity = 0.36' sentence and a fully documented version stating the exact computation and inputs, explaining in writing why the second version is the honest one.
slots.deliverable: Both the bare and fully-documented fidelity statements, with a written explanation of what information the bare version was missing.

slots.practicalActivity: Initialize a git repo for a toy gates.py file, make a commit with a vague message like 'fix bug', then make a second commit fixing the same kind of issue with a proper message explaining what was wrong and why the fix is correct (following the lesson's CNOT projector example), and tag the second commit with git tag -a.
slots.deliverable: The git log output showing both commits side by side for comparison, and the git tag -a command used to mark the corrected version.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Planning the Toolkit
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: A Mini Quantum Math Toolkit

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page scope document for the toolkit before writing any code: list exactly which gates (X, H, CNOT minimum), how many qubits (1-2), and what visualization you'll build, explicitly naming at least two features you are deliberately leaving out of scope, following the lesson's scope-creep warning.
slots.deliverable: A written scope document listing in-scope features, qubit count, and gate set, plus an explicit list of at least two out-of-scope features and why they're excluded for now.

lessons.title: Capstone: Build State-Vector & Gate Operations
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: A Mini Quantum Math Toolkit

slots.practicalActivity: Build gates.py and simulate.py exactly as shown (I, X, H, CNOT, kron_gate, zero_state, apply_gate, apply_gates), then run the Bell-state construction step by step, printing the intermediate state after H⊗I and the final state after CNOT, confirming both match the lesson's verified values.
slots.deliverable: The working gates.py/simulate.py code, plus the two printed intermediate/final state vectors matching [0.707107,0,0.707107,0] and [0.707107,0,0,0.707107].

lessons.title: Capstone: Build Measurement & Visualization
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: A Mini Quantum Math Toolkit

slots.practicalActivity: Add the probabilities, sample_measurements, and bloch_coordinates functions to your toolkit, run probabilities on your Bell state to confirm [0.5,0,0,0.5], and answer in writing the lesson's debugging question: if probabilities instead returned [0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25], which earlier step would you suspect first and why.
slots.deliverable: The working probabilities/bloch_coordinates code with the [0.5,0,0,0.5] output confirmed, plus a written debugging explanation for the hypothetical wrong-output scenario.

lessons.title: Capstone: Wrap-Up & Code Review
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: A Mini Quantum Math Toolkit

slots.practicalActivity: Write and run the three known-fact tests from this lesson (test_bell_state_construction, test_bell_state_probabilities, test_plus_state_bloch_coordinates) against your own toolkit code, confirm all three pass, then write out in words a fourth test for a single-qubit-only circuit and its exact expected numeric assertion.
slots.deliverable: The three passing test results from your own toolkit, plus a written description of a fourth single-qubit test and its expected exact numeric assertion.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can set up a reproducible scientific-Python environment and use NumPy, complex arithmetic, Matplotlib, and basic reproducibility/version-control practices to build, measure, and visualize real multi-qubit quantum states from scratch — demonstrated by a working, tested mini quantum-simulation toolkit that correctly constructs and verifies the Bell state.
